### Question 1

A pronoun works like a nickname: if someone says 'she,' you can only follow along because a real name was mentioned earlier. That earlier name is the antecedent, a word that literally means 'the one going before.' When the nickname shows up with no name behind it, the reader has to guess, and that guessing is exactly what vague pronoun reference causes in writing.

### Question 2

Cover the other person's name and read the sentence with the pronoun alone. 'Me reviewed the lab results' collapses immediately, so the form has to be 'I reviewed,' which gives you 'Maria and I reviewed.' The same test catches the opposite error: nobody says 'the instructor gave the results to I,' so that sentence needs 'me.'

### Question 3

The apostrophe in 'it's' is holding the place of letters that dropped out of 'is' or 'has.' So run the expansion out loud: 'The cell lost it is nucleus' breaks apart, which tells you the sentence needs 'its.' Possessive pronouns are already built to show ownership, so they never need an apostrophe to do that job.

### Question 4

Answer the question using 'he' or 'him' and see which one survives: 'The report should be addressed to him.' If 'him' fits, the question needs 'whom,' and the shared final m makes that easy to remember; if 'he' fits, use 'who.' The question mark and the passive verb are irrelevant here because case is decided by the job the pronoun does, not by the shape of the sentence around it.

### Question 5

Delete the -self word and see whether the sentence still stands. 'She injured' leaves the reader asking 'injured whom?', which shows the word was carrying the object slot, so it is reflexive. 'The instructor demonstrated the technique' loses nothing but emphasis when 'herself' goes, so that one was intensive. Identical word shapes, two different jobs, and the deletion test tells them apart every time.

### Question 6

Picture pointing at 'her' while two people stand side by side. Both can reasonably assume you mean them, and no rule of grammar decides it for them. That is ambiguous reference: the pronoun aims at a spot where more than one candidate is standing. The fix is not a grammar rule at all but a naming decision, such as 'the advisor said the schedule was full.'

### Question 7

'Each' asks the reader to picture the students one at a time, while 'their' pictures the whole group, so the two views of the same people clash. Rather than arguing over which pronoun to force in, widen the frame and write about all the students at once. Once the antecedent is truly plural, 'their' fits with no awkward 'his or her' and nothing to defend.

### Question 8

'Myself' behaves like a boomerang: it only works when 'I' is the one doing the throwing, as in 'I gave myself a break.' In this sentence the lab did the reporting, so there is no 'I' for the boomerang to return to. Drop the charge nurse and test what remains, and 'the lab reported the results to me' settles the case instantly.

### Question 9

Ask what the professor actually appreciated. Not the student as a person, but the arriving. Because 'arriving' is behaving like a thing here, you attach it to its owner the way you would attach any possession: 'his backpack,' not 'him backpack,' and so 'his arriving.' In casual speech 'him arriving' passes unnoticed, but graded academic writing expects the possessive.

### Question 10

A pronoun is supposed to point at one item on the shelf, but 'which' here gestures at the entire shelf, meaning everything said in the first half of the sentence. Readers usually reconstruct the idea, yet reconstruction is work, and in a long paragraph they can reconstruct it wrong. Naming the idea outright removes the guesswork and costs only a word or two.

### Question 11

'Neither of the applicants' sounds like it covers two people, but 'neither' means 'not one, taken one at a time,' so grammar counts it as singular and the phrase 'of the applicants' is only description. That is why the traditional pairing is with 'his or her.' Modern guides accept 'they' because it avoids the clunky double pronoun and covers people whose gender is unstated, so the sentence sits in a live disagreement rather than in plain error.

### Question 12

Finish the sentence in your head and the meaning appears. 'Than I' completes as 'than I supervised Jordan,' which compares two supervisors. 'Than me' completes as 'than the preceptor supervised me,' which compares two people being supervised. One letter of difference carries the whole comparison, so when the stakes are high, write the missing words out instead of trusting the reader to fill them in.
